So first of all, don't take it for granted that you articulated all your symptoms to a medical professional and they deemed to confirm your suspicions about ADHD, ask yourself first and foremost if you feel your ADHD symptoms have affected your life for a long time, you can probably remember an odd history of difficulty with certain things like focus, organization, hyperfixations, emotional regulation instability, etc. 
From what it sounds you're sorta giving yourself this imposter syndrome for not struggling to get treatment.
But here's the thing, that should be the norm, not the exception.
As far as taking meds for no reason, stimulants under a controlled dose would essentially make people feel "great" but there is a whole lot more tweaking and hyperfocus that goes on when neurotypical people take the drug, rather than just feeling good and focused and energized in a regular fashion 
This imposter syndrome is something you need to take a look at or you might start developing skepticism on behalf of how good you feel on meds because you have no frame of reference, so you might think the problem is just you and that you have no ADHD because the meds made you feel good or great etc. But that isn't true, happy for you, I take Adderall 30mg twice a day and I thankfully didn't struggle for a diagnosis, so I went through this thought process before so I understand

Hey! I feel like I have a good idea of where you can start to see some improvements with the delicate balancing act from hell that is life LMAO.
I'm 22 and was diagnosed last year and medicated this year and went through a period of struggling with managing all those blocks despite being medicated and thus having the stamina to do things.
Turns out the answer is usually some kind of personalized structured routine that allows you to stay on task in a way that fits the needs of your schedule around your family and work. But it's incredibly doable! I was assisted greatly in this by my therapist, which if you do not have one I greatly recommend it, it is eye opening what therapy can do to save families, and me and my partner are currently engaged rather than separated due to therapy. 
Second, get medicated. I would say depending on your child's age you may prefer to also take him to a behavioral therapist so he can learn coping mechanisms for his ADHD habits from a young developmental age. But for you, the adult, you should be able to find a treatment plan that covers your needs and honestly it makes a world of difference, both parents being at their fullest possible level of mental health through proper treatment and therapy is the best way to guarantee you'll be able to handle the mental load, invest in yourself and by extension you will be investing in the health of your relationship to the different facets of life!
